clue.text: If so, our shot scored wildly

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or broken up, so these letters are knocked out of shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A footballer's speculative effort somehow goes in, with a cheeky aside about luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scored' looks like a goal; it means written in a musical score, so the definition is a performance direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian musical direction telling players to perform with fury, i.e. a wild marking in the written part.

clue.text: Cases in intern scheme make better firm? Au contraire

indicators.note: the cases of words are their outer shells, so the first and last letters of each are taken

parts.note: to make better is to cure, as with an illness

explanation.surface: A cynical question whether an intern programme really strengthens a company, answered with a sceptical retort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Au contraire' (French: on the contrary) turns 'firm' into its opposite, so the definition is 'not firm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsteady or shaky is the opposite of firm, so 'firm, on the contrary' describes it.

clue.text: More faint from very fit runs

parts.note: an ague is a fit of fever and shivering
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone who was very fit now feels faint after a jog.
explanation.definitionFit: Comparative of an adjective meaning indistinct or hazy, matching a fainter outline or idea.

clue.text: European condition contributing to cuts in buildings

indicators.note: the condition word is contributed into the middle of the cuts word, so it goes inside

parts.note: to dice is to cut into cubes, so dices means cuts
if introduces a condition

explanation.surface: An EU stipulation is said to be behind spending cuts in public buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts' is a verb here (dices), not budget reductions.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand or large structures are buildings, the word usually used of imposing ones.

clue.text: Hot planet that's associated with fire

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
Earth is our planet

explanation.surface: A scorching world linked with flames, like a description of a hellish planet.
explanation.definitionFit: The floor of a fireplace is the spot where a domestic fire is laid and burns.

clue.text: Ark, one with a supply in American animals

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit in the American letters

parts.note: US is short for United States, so American

indicators.note: read as an adverb, supply means in a supple, bendy way, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Noah's Ark, plus some provisions, sitting among creatures in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' is not a noun here but the adverb from 'supple', bending ARK into KAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-tailed South American monkeys, so they are animals by example.

clue.text: Governess expected new article to be rejected

parts.note: something due is expected, as a train due at noon

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the article is read backwards

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A new governess was expected, but the paperwork was refused.
explanation.definitionFit: An older woman in charge of girls, especially in Spain, which makes her a chaperone or governess.

clue.text: Reading location wherein confused oldie enters bar

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go into the middle of the bar word

parts.note: to bar is to ban

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled and need sorting

explanation.surface: A muddled old man wanders into a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' tempts as the Berkshire town; it means somewhere to read: the Oxford University library.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Oxford library is a place where scholars go to read.

clue.text: Clutch bible, most frequently with cross

parts.note: the letter appearing most often in the word bible is B, twice
a rood is a cross or crucifix in a church

explanation.surface: Someone grips a Bible and a crucifix, as a devout person does often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most frequently' picks the commonest letter in 'bible', not a reading habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A batch of eggs or chicks hatched together is a clutch, also called a brood.

clue.text: Slowing down, head appearing after ceremony's over

indicators.note: the head word comes after the ceremony word

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony
nut is slang for head
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Someone shows up once the service has finished, with proceedings winding down.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian musical direction meaning held back, an immediate reduction of tempo.

clue.text: Denied access to bachelor in a car

indicators.note: the bachelor letters go in the car

parts.note: a Ford is a make of car
BA is a bachelor's degree, Bachelor of Arts

explanation.surface: A single man is refused entry to a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of a verb meaning prohibit, so it says someone was barred or refused entry.

clue.text: Before break of day, fairly settled

indicators.note: the fairly word comes before the letter from day

parts.note: fairly can mean squarely, as in fair and square

indicators.note: break of day is dawn, its very start, so the opening letter of day

explanation.surface: An argument patched up just before dawn, more or less calmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before break of day' looks like a time phrase; it orders the pieces, SQUARE then D.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt or dispute that has been paid off or resolved is squared up, i.e. settled.

clue.text: Several European countries vote for them in Brussels?

parts.note: the EU is a union of several European countries
X is the mark made on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: European nations casting votes for candidates in the EU capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Brussels is French-speaking, so 'them' is translated into French; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: French pronoun used after a preposition for 'them', as spoken in the Belgian capital.

clue.text: Unusually heroic chap in line to benefit

indicators.note: unusually means in an odd way, so the letters are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A remarkably brave man waiting for his reward.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who shares an inheritance with others stands in line to receive the estate.

clue.text: Following live broadcast of sex, a guest acts in a gracious way?

indicators.note: the scattered letters follow the live word

parts.note: to be is to live or exist

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A racy TV show in which a guest behaves graciously after a live sex broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: French phrase for noble gestures, actions done chivalrously for show.

clue.text: Extremely unusual rogue having a change of character in the future

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its ends, so the first and last letters
a character is a letter, so one letter of the rogue word is swapped

parts.note: a terror is a troublesome rogue, as in a little terror

explanation.surface: An odd scoundrel reforms his personality in times to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' means a letter, not personality: one R becomes I.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means lying beyond, further, or later than the present, hence future.

clue.text: To nearest and dearest it's common sense

indicators.note: common means shared, so the letters are the run found in both words, nearest and dearest

explanation.surface: Family members are told something is just common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The same three letters sit inside both 'nearest' and 'dearest', so they are what the two words have in common.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ of hearing stands for that sense itself, as in having a good ear.

clue.text: Organised activity hosted by wealthy regulars for a birthday

indicators.note: the event is hosted, held inside the regular letters
regular letters are every other one, here the 2nd, 4th and 6th

parts.note: an event is an organised activity

explanation.surface: A party thrown by rich people for someone's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regulars' looks like party guests; it picks the even letters of 'wealthy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, the ordinal names a particular birthday, as in celebrating her eleventh.

clue.text: Runs out of Shakespeare's first editions

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of Shakespeare's

parts.note: prints are printings or editions of a book

explanation.surface: A shop sells out of early Shakespeare folios.
explanation.definitionFit: Short fast races or dashes are runs, the noun sense of a quick dash.

clue.text: Agreement on track when Conservative is fully promoted

indicators.note: promoted means moved up, and fully means all the way to the top, so the letter goes to the front

parts.note: taken as written
to have the scent is to be on the track of quarry

explanation.surface: Party members agree on a direction when a Tory gets a big promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fully promoted' moves the C of ONSCENT right to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Permission or assent given to something counts as agreement.

clue.text: I choose pint to be consumed by old worker

indicators.note: consumed means swallowed, so the pint goes inside

parts.note: a worker ant is the classic crossword worker

explanation.surface: An old labourer drinking a pint and saying he gets to pick.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the voice of the answer: someone who opts says 'I choose'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who makes a choice, especially of nationality, is one who opts, so might say 'I choose'.

clue.text: A lass and a short lad with hands on hips?

parts.note: Kim is a girl's name

indicators.note: short means cut, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A girl and a small boy standing with arms bent.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes arms bent at the elbow with the hands resting on the hips.

clue.text: A certain style perhaps drawing Oscar after a month

indicators.note: the Oscar letter comes after the month

parts.note: drawing is an example of art
Dec is short for December
Oscar is O in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A sketch of an Oscar statuette made a month later.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1920s and 30s design movement is one example of a decorative style.

clue.text: ET upset first man on moon to some extent

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read upwards
only part of the name is used, the forename and first letter of the surname

parts.note: Neil Armstrong walked on the moon first, in 1969

explanation.surface: The film extraterrestrial is unsettled by Neil Armstrong's landing.
explanation.walkthrough: Only NEILA is used; 'upset' turns it round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the Spielberg film is an extraterrestrial, i.e. a being from another world.

clue.text: Communication system that's on course?

parts.note: the racecourse is the course, and bookmakers there signal odds with arm gestures

explanation.surface: A navigation or messaging system said to be working as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on course' looks like 'going to plan'; it means at a racecourse, where bookmakers signal odds with hand gestures (common in Britain).
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers' sign language at British race meetings is a way of passing odds across the crowd.

clue.text: More crafty with current bedfellow?

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
one who lies in bed is a lier

explanation.surface: A sly person who is more cunning than their partner in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bedfellow?' is a whimsical description: someone lying in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Comparative of an adjective for sly or cunning, meaning shrewder or trickier.

clue.text: Entering cover, soldiers step up

indicators.note: the soldiers enter the cover word, going inside it

parts.note: to incase, a variant of encase, is to cover
RE, the Royal Engineers, are soldiers

explanation.surface: Troops advancing into shelter, stepping up their pace.
explanation.definitionFit: To step something up is to raise or boost it, the verb meaning make bigger.

clue.text: Rigid objections overturned, then almost carried

indicators.note: overturned means turned back, so read backwards

parts.note: buts are objections, as in no ifs or buts

indicators.note: almost means just short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: borne means carried

explanation.surface: Firm objections are overruled, then nearly passed.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflexible in opinion, so a stubborn person is unbending or rigid.

clue.text: Listen to what may follow news feed's conclusion

parts.note: News at Ten is a British TV news bulletin, so the words 'at ten' may follow 'news'

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A tip to pay attention to whatever comes at the end of the newsfeed.
explanation.walkthrough: NEWS AT TEN is a long-running British evening TV news programme.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed or pay attention to someone is to listen to them.
